sheets.title: What does it mean to do work?
sheets.question: A porter carries a suitcase along a level platform all day and is exhausted. How much work did he do on the suitcase?
sheets.takeaway: work is the component of force along the displacement, with a sign

sheets.title: When the force changes, what replaces F d?
sheets.question: A spring stiffens as you pull it, and a gas pushes less hard as it expands. What is the work when the force is a curve?
sheets.takeaway: integrate the force along the path: the answer is a signed area

sheets.title: Which forces actually change the energy?
sheets.question: A block slides down a rough incline. Four forces act. Which of them can put energy in, which can only take it out, and which is powerless?
sheets.takeaway: audit each force separately; the normal force is almost always a zero

sheets.title: Why is Newton enough to get the work-energy theorem?
sheets.question: The theorem is usually quoted as a separate principle. Can you derive it from F = ma in one line?
sheets.takeaway: multiply Newton by a displacement: the theorem is Newton integrated once over space

sheets.title: Whose kinetic energy is it?
sheets.question: A 1 kg block moves at 4 m/s in the ground frame and 3 m/s in a train. Two observers, two kinetic energies. Is the law broken?
sheets.takeaway: kinetic energy is frame-dependent, so a work statement must name its frame

sheets.title: Where does the energy go when friction stops a block?
sheets.question: A block slides to rest. The work-energy theorem says the kinetic energy vanished. Energy is conserved, so where is it?
sheets.takeaway: friction turns mechanical energy into heat at f_k times the sliding distance

sheets.title: What is power, and why is it a dot product?
sheets.question: Two motors lift the same load through the same height; one takes twice as long. The work is identical. What differs?
sheets.takeaway: power is work per unit time, and at a given speed it is force times velocity

sheets.title: What happens when the power is held constant?
sheets.question: A car with a 100 kW engine at full throttle does not accelerate at a constant rate. What does its speed do?
sheets.takeaway: at constant power the acceleration must fall as the speed rises

sheets.title: Why does a hill cost so much more than a straight road?
sheets.question: A car cruising at 20 m/s needs 10 kW on the flat. On a 5° climb it needs much more. Where does the extra power go?
sheets.takeaway: climbing at speed v costs mgv sin theta just to gain height

sheets.title: What makes a force conservative?
sheets.question: Gravity and the spring let you keep a potential. Friction does not. What single test separates them?
sheets.takeaway: conservative means the work depends only on the endpoints, so a potential exists

sheets.title: Why can the zero of potential energy be anywhere?
sheets.question: A book on a shelf has 20 J of potential energy, or 5 J, or −100 J, depending on where you put the zero. Which is right?
sheets.takeaway: only differences of potential energy are physical, so the zero is yours to choose

sheets.title: Why is the spring energy half k x squared?
sheets.question: Pull a spring to extension x and the force has grown from zero to kx. Why is the stored energy not kx times x?
sheets.takeaway: the force is not constant, so the work uses its average, which is half the final value

sheets.title: Does the route up a hill change the energy?
sheets.question: Climb a hill by the gentle path or the steep one. The height gained is the same. Is the work by gravity the same?
sheets.takeaway: gravity charges by height gained, never by distance travelled

sheets.title: When may you write K + U = constant?
sheets.question: Energy conservation is quoted as a law. Under exactly what conditions is the mechanical version true?
sheets.takeaway: mechanical energy is constant exactly when no non-conservative force does net work

sheets.title: What can a potential-energy graph tell you at a glance?
sheets.question: Given U(x) and one number E, how much of the motion do you already know without solving anything?
sheets.takeaway: the graph is a map: where E crosses U is where the motion turns round

sheets.title: How do you get the force back from the energy?
sheets.question: You are given U(x) as a curve. Where is the force large, which way does it point, and where is it zero?
sheets.takeaway: force is minus the slope of the potential, so it points downhill

sheets.title: Energy or Newton: which method does the question want?
sheets.question: Two questions about the same loop: what is the speed at the top, and what is the normal force there? One is energy, one is not.
sheets.takeaway: energy answers speed and distance; forces answer time, acceleration and contact force

sheets.title: What changes when the system has two bodies?
sheets.question: Two blocks joined by a spring are pulled apart. The external work is 20 J, but the kinetic energy rises by only 12 J. Where are the other 8 J?
sheets.takeaway: internal work does not vanish: it moves energy into the spring, not out of the system

sheets.title: Why does a pump need more power than the water gains?
sheets.question: A pump lifts 100 kg of water per second through 20 m. The water gains 19.6 kW. The motor is rated 25 kW. Where did the rest go?
sheets.takeaway: efficiency is output over input, and every loss is a term you can name

sheets.title: Why does lifting a hanging chain cost more than its weight?
sheets.question: A chain is pulled up from a heap at constant speed. At height x the hanging weight is lambda x g, yet the pull must exceed it. Why?
sheets.takeaway: new links are accelerated from rest, so the pull carries a momentum-flux term

sheets.title: A spring launches a block onto a rough floor. How far does it go?
sheets.question: Compress a spring, release it, and let friction stop the block. Two energy stores and one loss. Which equation do you write?
sheets.takeaway: stored spring energy equals the friction work, and the loss is the bridge between them

sheets.title: What is the whole chapter in one picture?
sheets.question: Six ideas, a page of formulas and thirty-six questions. Which ideas actually carry the load?
sheets.takeaway: work is the unit of account, and every result is a ledger with a named loss

sheets.title: Why describe rotation with an angle at all?
sheets.question: Two points on a wheel, one near the rim and one near the hub, travel different distances in the same time. What do they share?
sheets.takeaway: every point shares the angle; only the radius converts it into a distance

sheets.title: What are the rotation equations for constant angular acceleration?
sheets.question: A flywheel spins up from rest at a constant 3 rad/s². How many turns does it make in 4 s?
sheets.takeaway: the linear equations with x, v, a replaced by theta, omega, alpha

sheets.title: Why is angular velocity a vector?
sheets.question: A wheel can spin about a vertical axis or a horizontal one, and the two are physically different. How does a single number capture that?
sheets.takeaway: omega points along the axis, and v = omega cross r gives the tangential speed

sheets.title: Why is circular motion at constant speed still accelerated?
sheets.question: The speedometer reads a constant 60 km/h on a roundabout. Is the car accelerating, and if so, in which direction?
sheets.takeaway: the speed is constant but the direction turns, so the velocity changes toward the centre

sheets.title: How much of the energy is actually available?
sheets.question: Two blocks collide. The total kinetic energy is 100 J, but only part of it can become heat or deformation. Which part?
sheets.takeaway: split the kinetic energy into drift of the centre of mass plus internal motion

sheets.title: Why does angular momentum keep a planet out of the Sun?
sheets.question: Gravity pulls inward with nothing to oppose it. Why does a planet not simply fall in?
sheets.takeaway: the angular term is a repulsive barrier made of kinetic energy, not a force

sheets.title: How far does a bouncing ball travel before it stops?
sheets.question: A ball is dropped from h and returns to e²h after each bounce. The bounces are infinite; is the total distance infinite too?
sheets.takeaway: two geometric series, one for distance and one for time, both with finite sums

sheets.title: Why does a rolling ball beat a sliding block downhill?
sheets.question: A ball and a block are released from the same height on the same slope. The block has no friction, the ball rolls. Which arrives first?
sheets.takeaway: a rolling body spends part of its energy on rotation, so it descends more slowly

sheets.title: Why is the block on a moving wedge slower than sqrt(2gh)?
sheets.question: A block slides down a smooth wedge that is free to slide on a smooth table. The textbook answer sqrt(2gh) must be wrong. Why?
sheets.takeaway: the wedge takes a share of the energy, so the block cannot have all of it

sheets.title: How much energy does it take to reach orbit?
sheets.question: Escape needs the full well depth. Orbit needs less, but not as little as you might hope. What fraction?
sheets.takeaway: low orbit costs half the escape energy, and the other half is the speed you keep

sheets.title: Where does the missing half of the work go?
sheets.question: A chain is pulled off a table at constant speed v. The power delivered is F v, but the energy in the chain grows more slowly. Where is the difference?
sheets.takeaway: links are jerked into motion inelastically, and the lost half is heat

sheets.title: Why does a spinning hoop make the bead climb?
sheets.question: A bead slides freely on a smooth hoop spinning about its vertical diameter. At high enough speed it leaves the bottom. Where does the energy come from?
sheets.takeaway: the hoop does work on the bead, and in the rotating frame that is one effective potential

sheets.title: What does the coefficient of restitution actually measure?
sheets.question: Two balls drop from the same height onto the same floor and bounce to different heights. What single number separates them?
sheets.takeaway: e is the ratio of relative speeds, so energy is multiplied by e squared per impact

sheets.title: Who pays for the kinetic energy of a flywheel?
sheets.question: A motor of constant power spins up a flywheel. The angular speed grows, but not linearly. Why, and who supplies the difference?
sheets.takeaway: at constant power the torque falls as one over omega, so the spin-up slows as root t

sheets.title: Can a force that is not there do work?
sheets.question: A ball hangs in an accelerating cart. In the cart frame it swings backward and gains speed. Which force did the work?
sheets.takeaway: in an accelerating frame the pseudo force does work, and the frame energy book stays closed

sheets.title: Is one closed loop enough to prove a force is conservative?
sheets.question: You are handed a force field and one closed loop. If the loop integral vanishes, may you conclude that a potential exists?
sheets.takeaway: one loop proves nothing; every loop must vanish, which is what the curl tests

sheets.title: Why does doubling speed need eight times the power?
sheets.question: A cyclist at 20 km/h is comfortable. At 40 km/h the same rider is exhausted. Why is the cost not twice?
sheets.takeaway: air resistance grows as the square of speed, and power as its cube

sheets.title: Where does the energy bookkeeping stop working?
sheets.question: The chapter treats mechanical energy as exact. At what speed, and at what scale, does the ledger need new terms?
sheets.takeaway: the classical ledger is a low-speed approximation, and the rest mass joins it at high speed

sheets.title: What if the speed changes as well as the direction?
sheets.question: A car on a curve brakes while turning. What is the total acceleration, and at what angle does it point?
sheets.takeaway: two perpendicular components: one changes the speed, one changes the direction

sheets.title: What if the angular acceleration is not constant?
sheets.question: A wheel slows under a torque that falls with time. The three rotation equations fail. What replaces them?
sheets.takeaway: integrate: omega is the area under alpha, theta the area under omega

sheets.title: How fast do two points on a wheel separate?
sheets.question: Two particles move on the same circle at different angular rates. How often do they meet, and what is their relative speed?
sheets.takeaway: relative angular rate is the difference, and relative speed is that times the radius

sheets.title: If the centripetal force is always inward, how does anything speed up?
sheets.question: On a vertical circle gravity has a tangential component; the tension never does. Which force changes the speed, and which only bends the path?
sheets.takeaway: a radial force does no work, so only the tangential component can change the speed

sheets.title: What speed does a bead have at the top of a loop?
sheets.question: A bead is released from rest at height h above the bottom of a smooth vertical loop. How fast is it at the top, and when does it leave the track?
sheets.takeaway: energy gives the speed at every angle; the track condition decides whether it stays on

sheets.title: Why must a string be launched faster than a rod?
sheets.question: The same mass, radius and release height. On a string it must be launched at sqrt(5gR); on a rod, sqrt(4gR) is enough. Where does the difference come from?
sheets.takeaway: a string can only pull, so its tension must stay positive; a rod can push

sheets.title: Why does a conical pendulum ignore the mass?
sheets.question: A bob whirls in a horizontal circle on a string of length L at angle theta. The tension depends on the mass, yet the period does not. Why?
sheets.takeaway: the two force equations both carry m, so it cancels out of the geometry and the period

sheets.title: What is the slowest safe speed on a banked corner?
sheets.question: Banking is designed for one speed. Too fast and the car slides up; too slow and it slides down. What sets both limits?
sheets.takeaway: friction can only widen the band around the design speed; it cannot create one

sheets.title: How does a wall of death hold a rider up?
sheets.question: A rider circles the inside of a vertical cylinder. The wall is vertical and there is no floor under the tyres. What holds the weight?
sheets.takeaway: the normal provides the centripetal force, and static friction on the vertical wall carries the weight

sheets.title: How tight is a curve that is not a circle?
sheets.question: A projectile path, a roller-coaster dip, a road bend: none is a circle. What is the radius at a point?
sheets.takeaway: the radius of curvature is the circle that matches the path locally, and v squared over it is the normal acceleration
